title: Residential vs Commercial Construction in NSW: What’s the Difference?
excerpt: Compare the checks for a NSW home renovation and an office FitOut: project scope, trade licences, approvals, insurance and delivery responsibilities.
metaTitle: Residential vs Commercial Construction in NSW | Your Office Space
metaDescription: Planning a NSW office FitOut? Compare residential and commercial project checks, including licences, insurance, approvals and who is responsible for the work.
author: Joe Kelley
body:
A home renovation and an office FitOut can involve similar trades. That does not make their contracts, approvals or delivery arrangements interchangeable.

For a business owner, the first step is to define the work and confirm who is responsible for each part. A label such as “commercial” is not enough to settle every requirement.

## Start with the building and the scope

Before requesting quotes, record:

- The building's current use and the proposed use of the premises.
- The rooms, finishes, furniture and services you want to change.
- What the landlord provides and what the tenant must arrange.
- Any residential or mixed-use parts of the building.
- Whether people will remain in the premises during the work.

Give this brief to your designer, certifier and proposed contractors. Ask them to identify the approvals and specialist advice the actual project needs. Do not assume that an existing office approval covers a new use or every alteration.

## Check licences for the actual work

NSW has different licence and registration categories. A business name or a general description such as “fitout specialist” does not tell you which work a contractor is authorised to undertake.

Specialist work can require a licence or certificate in residential, commercial and industrial premises. Electrical work, plumbing and air conditioning are examples. Check the relevant category and current licence details before appointing the trade.

For residential work, additional contractor-licensing rules can apply. Check the current NSW requirements against the scope and value of the work. Do not use this article as a licence assessment for a particular project.

## Separate coordination from construction

Agree the delivery roles in writing:

- **Client-side project manager:** helps the client organise the brief, design inputs, procurement, budget and programme within the agreed scope.
- **Builder or head contractor:** carries out and manages the construction work covered by its contract.
- **Specialist contractors:** perform the trade work they are appointed and appropriately authorised to do.
- **Designer and certifier:** provide their separately appointed design, approval or certification services.
- **Solicitor:** advises on legal obligations and contract wording.

These roles are not interchangeable. Check who appoints and pays each party, who supervises the work, and who deals with defects and changes.

## Confirm the insurance requirements

Ask which insurance applies, who holds it and what activities it covers. A policy name alone is not enough. Check the insured business, dates, limits and exclusions with the appropriate adviser.

Home building compensation requirements relate to eligible residential building work. Confirm the position for the actual project, especially where a building has mixed uses. Do not assume the word “commercial” answers every insurance question.

Public liability, contract works and professional indemnity may also need consideration. Employer obligations, including workers compensation where required, need their own checks. The construction contract is only one part of this review.

## Compare complete proposals

A useful comparison sets out more than the total price. Ask each delivery team to identify:

1. The drawings, specifications and quantities priced.
2. Included work, exclusions and provisional allowances.
3. Approval and landlord-consent responsibilities.
4. Services investigations and existing-building assumptions.
5. Access arrangements, working hours and the programme.
6. Payment stages, variations and delay procedures.
7. Testing, handover, defects and warranty arrangements.

Have your solicitor explain the contract and any statutory rights or duties that apply. Avoid assuming that a commercial contract removes all statutory protections, or that residential protections apply unchanged to an office project.

## Build the budget alongside the design

An attractive square-metre rate is only a starting point. Mechanical services, electrical capacity, room layouts and existing conditions can change the scope materially.

Develop the design and cost plan together. Confirm what is included before comparing options or committing to premises. Our [Newcastle FitOut cost guide](/blog/commercial-fitout-cost-newcastle-2026) explains the limits of early allowances.

## How Your Office Space helps

YOS provides [client-side commercial project management](/commercial-construction). We help coordinate the agreed planning and delivery workstream on the client's side. Appointed, appropriately licensed contractors perform construction and specialist trade work.

Read about [project management versus the builder's role](/blog/commercial-construction-project-manager-vs-builder-newcastle), or [discuss your office FitOut](/office-fitout) with our team.

*General planning information only. Requirements depend on the building, scope and delivery arrangements. Obtain project-specific advice from your solicitor, certifier, insurer and appropriately qualified contractors before committing.*
